title: kv-cache-access-pattern-attribution-wip
content:
Purpose:
Short working doc to capture experiments that try to attribute observed KV cache reuse/eviction behavior back to client access patterns. Trying to avoid repeating the same surface-level tests as previous docs (which looked mainly at global hit-rate and eviction pressure). This focuses on: per-client/per-route attribution, synthetic mixes that reproduce real churn, and microbenchmarks to isolate memory bandwidth vs CPU vs paging costs.

Context / why: 
- We keep seeing intermittent throughput collapses on tail-latency heavy workloads. Hit-rate looks OK at aggregate, but latency spikes correlate with eviction churn windows.
- Hypothesis: non-uniform access patterns (e.g., many short-lived sessions touching unique prefixes) cause pathological eviction churn and cause both increased paging (host<->device or host DRAM thrash) and increased memcpy/kernel overhead on GPU.

High-level goals:
- Build a small attribution pipeline to tag requests by route/session and compute reuse curves per-tag (reuse distance histogram, inter-arrival distribution).
- Recreate pathological mixes in a controlled microbenchmark and measure: hit-rate, eviction rate, paging events, memory bandwidth, and CPU/GPU utilization.
- Experiment with mitigations: per-route mini-quotas (pin hotsets), admission filters, probabilistic prefetch, and hysteresis in eviction thresholds.

What I ran so far (summary):
- Collected traces from prod for 72h (sampled 1/100 requests) across 3 routes: chat-realtime, batch-summarize, embedding-service. Added lightweight tag: route+session-id hash.
- Implemented offline reuse-distance extractor (python tool). Produced per-route reuse CDFs and inter-arrival histograms.
- Ran microbench harness (local kvm-based emulation) with synthetic clients: zipfian, uniform, session-affinity (long tail sessions), and churny-ephemeral (TTL 3-10 reqs).

Representative findings (raw/unpolished):
- chat-realtime: aggregate hit-rate 0.79 but top-10% of sessions account for 55% of hits; long tail sessions (55% sessions) have per-session hit-rate < 0.1.
- batch-summarize: high reuse within a job (0.92) but job-level churn when many concurrent jobs run; eviction spikes when >200 concurrent jobs.
- embedding-service: near-uniform keys => low cache usefulness.

Key observation that differs from prior notes: 
- Two different failure modes seen: (A) microburst eviction where a single large session or job pushes out a hotset and throughput drops for ~100-500ms while per-token latency increases; (B) gradual thrash where many ephemeral sessions collectively lower reuse and cause sustained high eviction rate.
- Mode A is relatively easy to mitigate with size-aware admission/pinning; Mode B is harder and drives memory bandwidth saturation on the host (observed increased page faults and heavy memcpy).

Profiling notes & commands used: 
- Tracing: capture request id -> KV lookup sequence (k=1..N). Wrote small tracer in C++ hooking into key lookup path with minimal instrumentation.
- Perf (on host): perf record -F 99 -g -- /path/to/serving-binary --cfg ... then perf report to find CPU contexts during eviction windows.
- GPU: nvprof / Nsight to check memcpy peaks during eviction/paging; recorded timeseries of cudaMemcpyAsync and kernel launches.
- OS metrics: vmstat/sar to see page-in rates; iostat to rule out disk I/O.

Microbenchmark config (reproducible commands):
- harness client: tools/kvbench/kvbench.py --pattern zipf --zipf-theta 0.9 --clients 120 --reqs 100000 --key-space 2M --key-size 64
- for session affinity: kvbench.py --pattern sessions --session-ttl 5 --session-count 40 --hotset 10000
- runtime flags: --cache-size-entries 500k --eviction-policy lru-approx --eviction-batch 64 --page-threshold 0.8

Example outputs (trimmed):
- zipf (theta 0.9): hit-rate 0.68, eviction-rate 1.9k/s, mean lookup latency 8.2ms, 99p 45ms.
- sessions (ttl=5): hit-rate 0.35, eviction-rate 6.3k/s, mean lookup 12.7ms, 99p 120ms. Paging events (host) increased 4x in sessions case.

Memory bandwidth & paging observations: 
- During high-eviction runs we see sustained memcpy bursts (on GPU builds) that align with eviction batches being transferred for spill/paging. This coincides with elevated PCIe (or NVLink) utilization and host-side memcpy CPU spikes.
- Host DRAM working set oscillates more in the churny-ephemeral tests: OS reports higher page reclaim activity; swap usage climbs (in our emulation where we allowed spill-to-host). In prod we do not swap, but we do see HBM pressure and NVMM activity in private deployments.
- Hypothesis: repeated evictions cause repeated zeroing/initialization + memcopy which costs both CPU cycles and memory BW; when combined with many concurrent clients this becomes the dominant limiter, not pure compute.

Eviction policy experiments (notes):
- Default LRU-approx: stable under zipf heavy-hotset, but poor in churny-ephemeral mixes because it still cycles many entries frequently.
- CLOCK with reference count window: reduced churn by ~20% for session-affinity case but slightly worse for pure zipf.
- Per-route pinned quotas (reserve X% of capacity per route): eliminates Mode A failures but needs careful sizing and can reduce overall hit-rate if mis-sized.
- Admission filter (tiny LFU sketch to avoid admitting one-off keys): helpful. Sketch size tradeoffs need tuning (experimented with 8KB and 64KB sketches).

Preliminary mitigation that looks promising: 
- Two-tier cache: small fast L1 pinned for per-route hotset (configurable), larger shared L2 with relaxed eviction (batched eviction + probation). L1 prevents single-job displacement.
- Add hysteresis to eviction thresholds so we don't immediately reclaim entries as soon as free ratio drops slightly (reduces oscillation).
- Lightweight per-session admission + early eviction for keys with TTL < N requests.

Data artifacts attached (where to find): 
- traces: s3://redwood-obs/kv-traces/2025-10/kv-trace-72h-sample-1.json.gz
- microbench outputs: gs://redwood-eng-testing/kvbench/2025-11/* (csvs with time-series)
- perf recordings: internal perf-store:perf-rt-10-2025

Open questions / TODOs: 
- How to choose L1 size per route automatically? Propose: compute skew ratio (top-1% contribution) and allocate cap proportional to that skew; need to test fairness across many routes.
- Can we cheaply detect churn-onset in production (cheap signal)? Candidate signals: rising eviction-rate per-second, sudden drop in local reuse-curve slope, spike in memcpy calls. Need to prototype runtime detector (thresholds, window sizes).
- If we add admission filter based on recent frequency, what's the cost of false negatives for legitimate sparsely-accessed keys? Test with hybrid workloads.
- On private deployments we saw more paging-like behavior due to limited HBM and slower interconnects; need to run similar microbench on staged A100 and AMD MI250 instances to compare.

Immediate next steps (next 2 weeks):
- Build the production-safe churn detector (lightweight counters + EWMA) and add to serving binary behind flag.
- Add per-route L1 prototype (configurable via route metadata) and run A/B with canary.
- Run targeted microbench on cloud GPU pools with realistic model run (long sequence lengths) to validate GPU memcpy patterns and NVLINK saturation.
- Summarize results in follow-up doc with clear perf-vs-cost tradeoffs.

Notes to self / rough TODOs (quick list):
- [ ] Push small profiler hook to PR 449 (Marcelo already has draft).
- [ ] Add session-id tagging to prod sampling pipeline (JIRA-RT-769) and run 7d sample.
- [ ] Bake in admission filter with configurable sketch size and expose telemetry for tuning.
- [ ] Run durability test for L1 pinned hotset under overload.

Unresolved assumptions (callout):
- We assume host-to-device transfers are the dominant source of extra latency during eviction windows; need precise breakdown (host memcpy vs kernel time).
- Many numbers above are from emulation; real prod hardware (different HBM/PCIe/NVLink topologies) may shift which mitigation is best.

If you want to reproduce: start with the harness and the same flags (see commands above). For quick experiments use --key-space 200k to speed up runs.

If you have ideas for cheap runtime signals to detect churn/oscillation, ping me.

-- Lina
